processing: A fine bud-and-leaf green tea, fixed with heat and dried without oxidation; published accounts give no detailed steps.
harvest_season: Little is documented about exact picking dates; as with other Zhejiang greens, early spring tea is the prized part of the year.
appearance_dry: Fine, tender, upright leaves in jade green with visible white down.
appearance_wet: Tender green shoots opening into intact clusters.
taste_profile: A clean lasting fragrance with a fresh mouth and a sweet return, in the high-mountain mist style.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for a tender Zhejiang green: a glass or gaiwan with the lid off, and water well below the boil.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring green, as is usual for its class, and best within the year. As with other greens, earlier picking generally costs more. Look for the harvest year on the pack.
description:
Wanghai Cha is the signature green tea of Ninghai county in Ningbo, and a young one. The name means sea-gazing: it grows on Wanghai Gang, a high ridge in the outliers of the Tiantai range, from which the East China Sea can be seen.

The producer describes a misty, high-altitude site near the Nanxi hot springs. That setting is the selling point here, and it fits the wider idea of high-mountain green tea, though the claims about purity come from the maker itself.

The dry leaf is fine, upright and downy. The cup is described as clear and pale green with a lasting clean scent and a fresh, sweet finish. Treat it gently: cool water and short contact, typical of tender greens.

It is a named regional brand, so packaging is usually clear about origin. As with any green tea, freshness comes first, so buy the current year.
history:
By the producer's own account the tea was created in 1980 and recognised as a provincial famous tea in 1984, which makes it a modern creation and not an old tribute tea.

Ningbo press lists it among the first group of ten famous Zhejiang teas, and provincial tea tourism promotion features it alongside Pubu Xianming and Fenghua Qu Hao. It also appears as a tribute tea in a Chinese television fantasy, which is fiction and no evidence of age.
